meta.title: Who really said "I think, therefore I am"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely Descartes. He wrote it in French ("Je pense, donc je suis") in Part IV of the Discourse on the Method (1637), not as the Latin "Cogito, ergo sum."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I think, therefore I am'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Descartes — but he wrote it in French in the 1637 Discourse on the Method, not as the Latin "Cogito, ergo sum" people picture.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely his. Descartes wrote it in French as “Je pense, donc je suis” in the first paragraph of Part IV of the Discourse on the Method (1637). “I think, therefore I am” is the standard English translation — the form popularised by the Haldane & Ross 1911 edition.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “I think, therefore I am” — standard English form (Haldane & Ross, 1911)

source.excerpt: …I observed that whilst I thus wished to think all things false, it was absolutely essential that the ‘I’ who thought this should be somewhat; and remarking that this truth, ‘I think, therefore I am,’ was so certain and so assured that all the most extravagant suppositions brought forward by the sceptics were incapable of shaking it, I came to the conclusion that I could receive it without scruple as the first principle of the Philosophy for which I was seeking.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section attributes “I think, therefore I am” / “Je pense, donc je suis” to the Discours de la Méthode (1637).
Wikipedia’s “Cogito, ergo sum” confirms the phrase “first appeared (in French) … in the first paragraph of its fourth part,” and that the Latin form came later.
The same article notes John Veitch’s 1850 translation rendered it “I think, hence I am,” while the Haldane & Ross 1911 translation established the now-standard “I think, therefore I am.”
source.excerptNote: Part IV of the Discourse, in the Haldane & Ross (1911) translation. The French original reads “…cette vérité, je pense, donc je suis…”

sourceLink.text: Wikipedia: Cogito, ergo sum — sources and translation history

source.rightsNote: The French original was first published in 1637 and is long in the public domain. The standard English wording “I think, therefore I am” comes from the Haldane & Ross translation of 1911 — also public domain in the United States (published before 1931).

author.name: René Descartes
author.heading: About René Descartes
author.bio: René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French philosopher, mathematician and scientist often called the father of modern philosophy. In the Discourse on the Method (1637) and Meditations on First Philosophy (1641) he pursued a program of radical doubt, arriving at the thinking self as the one thing that cannot be doubted. He also gave us Cartesian coordinates, linking algebra and geometry.

misattribution.heading: The common misconception
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Descartes is correct — but almost everyone misremembers how and where he said it.

items.scope: “He wrote ‘Cogito, ergo sum’ in the Discourse”
items.who: Descartes — but in French, not Latin
items.why: In the 1637 Discourse on the Method he wrote “je pense, donc je suis” in French. The Latin “cogito, ergo sum” appears only later — in the 1644 Latin edition of the Discourse and, as “ego cogito, ergo sum,” in the Principles of Philosophy (1644, Part I, art. 7).

items.scope: “It’s the famous line from the Meditations”
items.why: His best-known work, the Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), never states the familiar phrase; there the certainty is expressed as “Ego sum, ego existo” — “I am, I exist”.

misattribution.truthLine: So: really Descartes, really his idea and his words — but the original is French (“je pense, donc je suis”) in the 1637 Discourse, and the Latin “cogito, ergo sum” came seven years later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Descartes was hunting for one belief that could survive total, systematic doubt — a bedrock certain enough to rebuild all knowledge on. Even a deceiving demon, he reasoned, could not trick him into thinking he existed if he did not: the very act of doubting proves a doubter. That single fixed point — “I think, therefore I am” — became the first principle of modern Western philosophy.
The line marks a turning inward: certainty is founded not on the external world or authority but on the thinking self. It is why Descartes is so often called the father of modern philosophy.
context.pull: The one thing doubt cannot touch is that there is someone doing the doubting.
